title: Borderlines
blurb: Drop each legal instrument onto the regime that wields it, then read what actually restricts the data crossing that border.
source: Chapple CISSP SG 10ed ch.4 · outline 1.4 (legal, regulatory, and compliance issues; transborder data flow; privacy law)

map.title: Borderlines
map.prompt: Match each instrument to the regime that enforces it — then read what it really does to data crossing that border.
map.note: Markers sit at the real coordinates of each regime's seat or geographic center, projected onto a Miller-style world map; labels in dense regions are nudged clear of their marker. Instruments, transfer rules and effective dates are authored from Chapple CISSP SG 10ed ch.4 and the Moore Domain 1 objective notes.

legend.label: Omnibus privacy law with transfer restrictions

jurisdictions.name: European Union
obligations: One harmonized regime across every member state, replacing the older Data Protection Directive
Reaches any organization anywhere that processes the personal data of people in the EU
Personal data may leave only toward an adequacy-listed destination or under approved safeguards such as SCCs or Binding Corporate Rules
A discovered breach must be reported to the supervising authority inside 72 hours
jurisdictions.tell: The regime that exports its own rulebook: lawful transfer runs through an adequacy finding or contract-grade safeguards, and the obligation follows the person the data describes, not the server it sits on.

jurisdictions.name: United States (federal)
jurisdictions.effective: sectoral statutes from 1974 onward; CLOUD Act 2018
obligations: No single omnibus federal privacy statute — protection attaches by sector: health records, financial customers, children online
US providers can be compelled to hand over data they control regardless of which country physically stores it
Bilateral executive agreements give partner governments reciprocal access, with a mechanism for providers to challenge an order
Breach duties arrive piecemeal through sector rules and state notification laws rather than one national trigger
jurisdictions.tell: A patchwork keyed to industry rather than to the individual — and its law-enforcement reach statute follows the provider across borders, which is the opposite direction from a data-localization rule.

jurisdictions.name: California
obligations: Binds for-profit businesses over the revenue or data-volume thresholds; nonprofits and government agencies sit outside it
Residents can know, delete, correct, opt out of sale or sharing, limit use of sensitive data, and demand equal treatment
Duties flow down to service providers and contractors through their processing agreements
One state's consumer statute doing national work, because out-of-state businesses meet its thresholds
jurisdictions.tell: A single US state reaching past its border through revenue and volume thresholds — the strongest evidence that the US answer to privacy is a patchwork, not an omnibus law.

jurisdictions.name: China
obligations: Explicit consent for processing and aggregation, withdrawable by the individual
Collection limited to what the stated purpose genuinely needs
Individuals hold access, correction, deletion and breach-notice rights
Outbound transfers are restricted: personal data leaves the country only after state-set conditions are satisfied
jurisdictions.tell: GDPR-shaped on consent and rights, but its transfer chapter points inward — the state gates the exit, which is localization pressure rather than an adequacy bridge.

jurisdictions.name: South Africa
obligations: Eight named conditions for lawful processing, from accountability through limits on further processing
Consent from the data subject, or a parent or guardian where the subject is a child
Tight handling rules for special categories such as race, religion, union membership and political life
Cross-border transfer allowed only where the receiving country's protection resembles its own; the Information Regulator enforces
jurisdictions.tell: Eight enumerated conditions and a dedicated regulator — its border test asks whether the destination's law looks like its own, a similar-protection rule rather than a contract mechanism.

jurisdictions.name: Canada
obligations: Federal statute governing how private-sector organizations handle personal information in commercial activity
The collecting organization stays answerable for the data even after handing it to a processor elsewhere
Consent, purpose and safeguard duties travel with the information through the transfer
jurisdictions.tell: The commercial-activity statute where accountability is sticky: outsourcing the processing never outsources the responsibility, wherever the processor sits.

jurisdictions.name: EU–US corridor
obligations: Third attempt at an adequacy bridge for EU-to-US flows: Safe Harbor came first, then Privacy Shield
Privacy Shield was struck down by the EU's top court in the Schrems II ruling of July 2020
US companies self-certify to the framework; only certified recipients enjoy the adequacy basis
Without a bridge like this, EU personal data heading to the US needs SCCs or another safeguard case by case
jurisdictions.tell: The corridor that keeps dying in court — Safe Harbor fell, Privacy Shield fell to Schrems II, and this framework is the current adequacy bridge holding EU-to-US flows open.

jurisdictions.name: OECD
obligations: Eight principles, running from limits on collection and fidelity to stated purpose through safeguards, openness, individual participation and accountability
Urges members not to raise unjustified obstacles to transborder data flows
No enforcement arm — the principles bind only as far as members legislate them
jurisdictions.tell: Principles, not penalties: the eight-point vocabulary most national privacy laws later borrowed, paired with an explicit plea to keep data moving across borders.

jurisdictions.name: Wassenaar Arrangement states
obligations: Multinational, voluntary export-control regime for conventional arms and dual-use technology, cryptography included
Each participating state implements the control lists through its own national export law
Nothing in it protects personal data — it polices the technology itself crossing the border
jurisdictions.tell: Not a privacy instrument at all: it controls what crosses the border when the export is the technology — and only as strongly as each member writes it into national law.

jurisdictions.name: Council of Europe signatories
obligations: The Budapest treaty: signatory states harmonize their computer-crime offences
Creates cross-border cooperation channels for investigations and evidence
Binds the governments that sign it, not the companies operating under them
jurisdictions.tell: A treaty about prosecutions rather than privacy — it moves offences and evidence across borders by obligating governments to cooperate, and never binds a company directly.
